meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'естра'). Common feminine noun meaning 'sister' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He gave our sister a flat.

examples.text: Ты бы брал пример с сестры! Сестра умная, серьёзная, старательная.
examples.trans: You should follow your sister's example! Your sister is smart, serious, and hardworking.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мысл'). Common masculine noun meaning 'sense, meaning' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: What do you mean? Where is Mishkin?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.
Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'hand; arm' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'even', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very, very much', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'нравиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to be liked, to please', paired with 'нравиться'.

examples.trans: Don't be afraid, you'll like it.

examples.text: А придётся! Не бойся, тебе понравится.
examples.trans: Well, you'll have to! Don't be afraid, you'll like it.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'okay', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А я пойду принесу выпить, окей?
examples.trans: I will go grab us something to drink, okay?

examples.text: Я уже всё решил. Одну треть на кладбище, две трети над океаном.
examples.trans: I've already sorted it all out. One third goes to the cemetery, two thirds over the ocean.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лушать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to listen', paired with 'послушать'.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

examples.trans: She has been doing dance since childhood.

examples.text: Видела я твой танец. Балерина из тебя никакая!
examples.trans: I saw your dance. You're no ballerina at all!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'love' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я умоляю вас, доктор! Это всё ради любви!
examples.trans: I beg you, Doctor! This is all for love!

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'чинаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to begin, to start', paired with 'начаться'.

examples.text: Спасибо, теперь для нас начинается новая жизнь.
examples.trans: Thank you, now a new life begins for us.
Our work is only just beginning.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on, go on', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Go on, tell me: how much is here?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'годить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'wait'.

examples.trans: Wait. Maybe everything will still work out.

examples.text: Погоди, нам нужна более объективная оценка.
examples.trans: Wait, we need a more objective opinion.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
